title: Keeping things warm or cold by wrapping them
keyIdea: Wrapping something in a thick, fluffy material slows heat moving in or out. A warm drink in a woolly cover stays warm for longer, and an ice cube in a sock stays frozen for longer. Wrapping does not make heat: a coat keeps your own body's warmth in.
familyTip: Try the sock test: put one ice cube in a clean sock and one on a plate, and check every few minutes. Ask which will melt first before you start. Then talk about why a woolly hat keeps your head warm: your head makes the warmth and the hat keeps it in.

visual.caption: Does the wrapping keep it warm or keep it cold? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Ice lolly in a cool bag
Frozen peas in a cool box

lab.caption: Flagship lab: ice cube race, test three wrappers, add layers until playtime, sort warm and cold, dress for snow.

kid: Put one ice cube in a sock. Leave one ice cube bare. Which melts first? The bare one! The sock keeps the warm air away from the ice.
A woolly hat is not hot by itself. Your head makes the warmth. The hat keeps your warmth in, so you feel cosy.
Thick, fluffy things keep heat in best. A woolly scarf works better than thin paper or a net with holes.
Wrapping works for cold things too. Ice cream in a cool bag stays cold for longer. But wrapping never makes a drink hotter than it was.
adult: Ages 4 to 5. Development Matters (2021) asks Reception children to explore the natural world, describe what they see and talk about the properties of materials and how they change. This topic starts thermal insulation: thick materials that trap air slow heat moving in or out. In England's National Curriculum, choosing materials for a job comes in Year 2, and conductors and insulators come later. Key words: warm, cold, wrap, keep in, keep out, melt.

Do the tests at home. Wrap one ice cube in a sock and leave one bare, then check every 5 minutes. Pour two cups of warm water, wrap one in a tea towel and feel them after 15 minutes. Ask your child to predict first, then talk about what happened and why.

Common mistakes: thinking wool or a coat makes heat, so a wrapped ice cube will melt faster; thinking wrapping makes a drink hotter than it started; thinking wrapping only works for warm things; and thinking any wrapper works, thin or thick. These ideas are well documented in research on children's ideas about heat, so be careful to say 'keeps the warmth in' rather than 'the coat is warm'.

In the lab your child puts a sock on one ice cube and watches the bare one melt first, wraps three cups of cocoa in a scarf, thin tissue and a net, then adds layers until a cup stays warm until playtime. They sort wrapped things into 'stays warm' and 'stays cold', and dress a child in the snow, finding that a coat would not warm a snowman.

practice.prompt: One ice cube is in a woolly sock. One is bare. Which melts first?
practice.hint: Does the sock make heat, or does it keep the warm air away?
practice.explain: The bare one melts first. The sock keeps the warm air away from the ice, so the wrapped cube stays frozen longer.

practice.prompt: You wrap 2 ice cubes in woolly socks and leave {n} ice cubes bare. How many ice cubes melt first?
practice.hint: Which cubes have nothing to keep the warm air away from them?
practice.explain: The {n} bare cubes melt first. The 2 in socks stay frozen longer because the socks keep the warm air away.

practice.prompt: A cup has {n} woolly layers round it. You add 1 more layer. How many layers keep the warmth in now?
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1} layers. More thick layers keep the cocoa warm for longer.

practice.prompt: Which wrapper keeps warm cocoa warm for longest?
practice.hint: Thick, fluffy things trap air. Which one is thick and fluffy?
practice.explain: The woolly scarf is thick and fluffy, so it traps air and slows the warmth getting out. Thin tissue and a holey net let it out.

practice.prompt: Where does the warmth inside your coat come from?
practice.hint: Is a coat warm when it hangs on a hook?
practice.explain: Your body makes the warmth. The coat keeps it in. A coat on a hook is not warm by itself.

pool.prompt: Can a cool bag keep ice cream cold?
choices: Yes, it keeps the warmth out
No, wrapping only keeps things warm
No, it makes the ice cream melt
pool.hint: Wrapping slows heat moving in as well as out.
pool.explain: Yes. The cool bag slows the warmth getting in, so the ice cream stays cold for longer.

pool.prompt: Warm soup goes into a flask. Later you open it. The soup is…
choices: A bit cooler, but still warm
pool.hint: Can wrapping add heat? Or does it only slow the cooling?
pool.explain: The flask slows the cooling, so the soup is still warm but a little cooler. Wrapping never makes it hotter.

pool.prompt: Zoe puts a coat on a snowman to warm it up. What happens?
pool.hint: The snowman makes no warmth. What does the coat keep out?
pool.explain: The coat keeps the sun's warmth out, so the snowman melts more slowly. A coat cannot make heat.

pool.prompt: You wrap {n} cups in thick scarves and leave 1 cup bare. How many cups stay warm for longer?
pool.hint: Only the wrapped cups keep the warmth in for longer.
pool.explain: The {n} wrapped cups stay warm longer. The bare cup cools fastest.

pool.prompt: Can bubble wrap keep a drink warm?
choices: Yes, its air bubbles slow the heat
No, only clothes keep things warm
pool.hint: What do thick, fluffy things and bubble wrap both hold? Air.
pool.explain: Bubble wrap traps air in its bubbles, so it slows heat moving out, just like a woolly scarf.

pool.prompt: Ali says, 'My woolly hat is warm, so it will melt an ice cube.' Is he right?
choices: No, the hat keeps warmth out of the ice
Yes, if the hat is red
pool.hint: Is a hat warm when nobody is wearing it?
pool.explain: A hat is not hot by itself. Wrapped round ice, it keeps the warm air away, so the ice melts more slowly.

pool.prompt: Which keeps a baby warmest outside on a cold day?
pool.hint: Which one is thick and traps air?
pool.explain: The thick blanket traps air and keeps the baby's own warmth in. Thin paper and a net let the warmth out.

pool.prompt: You wrap {n} ice lollies in towels on a sunny day. What happens to them?
pool.hint: The towel slows the warmth getting in.
pool.explain: The towels keep the warm air away, so all {n} lollies stay frozen for longer.

pool.prompt: Why do we wear a coat in the snow?
choices: To keep our own warmth in
pool.hint: Who makes the warmth: you or the coat?
pool.explain: Our bodies make warmth. The coat keeps it in, so we stay warm in the snow.
